summary: Summarizes techniques for web page authors to detect which MIME types a user's browser can handle. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A website wants to know which kinds of files your browser can open before sending one. This describes ways to find out.

questions: how to detect browser mime type handlers
how to detect mime type handlers
subtitle: Methods to detect MIME types supported by a user's browser

tldr.problem: Web page authors need to know which MIME types a user's browser can handle before sending content, but browsers often do not accurately report their capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes several techniques: checking the HTTP Accept header, using JavaScript to query the browser's mimeTypes array, reading the Windows Registry via ActiveX for older Internet Explorer versions, and using ECML fields for e-commerce.
tldr.outcome: Authors can combine these methods in a decision tree to determine handler availability and serve appropriate content, though this approach became obsolete with better standards.

today: RFC 2936 is informational and was always intended as a temporary guide for the pre-standardization era of 2000. Modern content negotiation uses the HTTP Accept header more reliably and newer standards developed in the W3C and IETF.

sections.title: The Problem of Unknown Capabilities
sections.content:
Web servers often do not know what kinds of files a user's browser can handle. When a server sends content in a MIME type the browser cannot process, the result is a broken experience: the user is prompted to choose what to do with the file, or the browser fails to display it properly. The problem arises because handlers for specialized MIME types—such as application/iotp for Internet Open Trading Protocol, application/vnd.vrml for VRML graphics, or streaming media handlers—are optional and not always installed.

This RFC summarizes practical techniques available as of early 2000 for web authors to detect which MIME handlers are present on a user's system before choosing what content to send.
sections.plainLanguage: A website wants to know: can your browser handle this kind of file? It can check a few places to find out.

sections.title: The HTTP Accept Header
sections.content:
The HTTP request header called Accept is designed to list the MIME types the client supports. According to the HTTP specification, the server should respect this header. However, the RFC notes a critical problem: many browsers at the time simply sent the generic value */*, meaning they accept anything, which provides no useful information about specific handlers.

When a specific MIME type appears explicitly in the Accept header, it is generally safe to assume the browser has a handler for it installed. The RFC recommends that MIME handler vendors help by adding their types to the Accept header when the software is installed.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser can tell the server which file types it understands. But many browsers just say they understand everything, which is not helpful.

sections.title: JavaScript-Based Detection
sections.content:
Most browsers of the era supported JavaScript, a scripting language that can run inside web pages and probe the browser's environment. JavaScript provides access to a navigator.mimeTypes array, which lists the MIME types the browser has handlers for.

A web page can use JavaScript to check whether a specific MIME type exists in this array and conditionally display different content based on the result. The RFC includes example JavaScript code that detects the browser version, operating system, and installed handlers. However, this method has limitations: JavaScript must be enabled, and in older Internet Explorer versions (3 and 4), the mimeTypes array was either absent or always empty.
sections.plainLanguage: JavaScript code inside a web page can ask the browser: "Do you have a handler for this type of file?" The browser tells it yes or no.

sections.title: Windows Registry and ActiveX
sections.content:
Older Microsoft Internet Explorer versions did not report MIME handlers correctly via JavaScript. The RFC describes how to use ActiveX controls—compiled programs that run inside the browser—to query the Windows Registry directly. The Registry stores handler information under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\MIME\Database\Content Type\. By checking whether a key exists for a specific MIME type, the code can determine if a handler is installed.

The RFC provides example code that opens Registry keys to test for IOTP handlers. This technique is Windows-specific and browser-specific, but it was necessary for Internet Explorer 3 and 4 compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: On Windows, file type information is stored in a database called the Registry. Special programs (ActiveX controls) can check that database to see what file types the computer understands.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly warns that reading the Windows Registry is a security risk. An ActiveX control can examine the user's computer without obvious consent, and a malicious control could extract or modify sensitive system information.

More broadly, JavaScript and especially ActiveX are powerful and dangerous. A compromised web page could invisibly damage a client system. The RFC emphasizes that security should depend on encryption of the channel between browser and server (such as TLS), not on these detection techniques alone.
sections.plainLanguage: These methods can learn about what is on your computer. A bad website could misuse that power to spy on you or harm your system.

sections.title: The Decision Tree
sections.content:
The RFC describes combining these techniques into a decision tree: first check the HTTP Accept header, then try JavaScript detection if available, then ActiveX on Windows-based Internet Explorer, and finally apply a default assumption. This multi-method approach maximized coverage across the browsers deployed in 2000.

Today, this approach is historical. Modern HTTP standards include better mechanisms for content and capability negotiation, and most of the concerns that motivated this document have been addressed by browser improvements and standardization. The RFC itself acknowledges that it was intended as a temporary solution until better standards became widespread.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can try multiple tricks in order: check the Accept header, ask JavaScript, ask the Registry. Whichever method works determines what to send.
